newsitem.title: UK: IBCA assigns Egypt investment grade rating.
newsitem.headline: IBCA assigns Egypt investment grade rating.

text.p: LONDON, Aug 19 - IBCA, the European credit rating agency, today assigned a long-term rating of BBB- to the Arab Republic of Egypt.

The rating applies to all senior, unsecured foreign currency debt issues, including any forthcoming eurobond and sets a ceiling for IBCA rated banks and corporates in Egypt. A short-term foreign currency rating of A3 will apply to issues with a maturity of up to one year.
IBCA also assigned an A- long-term local currency rating, applicable to government issues in Egyptian pounds.

The agency said that Egypt was now a net external creditor. This debt position is the culmination of substantial debt forgiveness led by the United States in the wake of Egypt's role in the Gulf war, five years of consecutive surpluses on the current account of the balance of payments, and a substantial build-up of foreign exchange reserves now worth more than a year's imports.

Moreover, external debt is primarily long-term concessional finance with low debt service. Egypt's relative financial strength is also underpinned by a steady decline in the fiscal deficit, macro-economic stabilisation and low inflation.

The internal political situation has also begun to improve. The security threat of the militant Islamists has been overcome, and the new administration of Prime Minister Ghanzouri is making efforts to alleviate the social conditions in which it had grown. The succession to President Mubarak is likely to be smooth, and the authorities are determined to prevent the entanglement of Egypt in current Israeli-Palestinian tensions. This stance is underpinned by US support.

The main constraint on the rating is the weakness of Egypt's real economy, which is reflected in low investment and in the low growth of foreign exchange receipts. Non-oil exports have been particularly weak.

State-owned enterprises are still important and the private sector is only now shaking off a legacy of state intervention and protection. Structural reform, particularly privatisation, has lagged behind Egypt's success in stabilisation. IBCA warns that growing receipts, both from tourism and from non-oil exports, will be important to prevent an excessive current account deterioration as traditional sources, such as the Suez canal, oil and aid, wane.

Against this, the Ghanzouri administration has made increasing efforts to address structural impediments, and the recent acceleration of privatisation demonstrates its good faith. Combined with Egypt's very low labour costs and its improving access to world markets, particularly the European Union, reform should help Egyptian firms to modernise and become competitive on the non-price factors which are probably the chief obstacle to export growth.

NOTES: IBCA's rating follows a wide two rating notch split in the Egyptian ratings of the two US agencies. The Arab Republic of Egypt was assigned a speculative grade rating of Ba2 by Moody's Investors Service in October 1996, and this has just been put on rating watch for an upgrade. Standard & Poor's assigned an investment grade rating of BBB- in January 1997.
